claims.text: The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy is equimolar, single-phase, solutionized, and chemically disordered.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has moderate hardness and strength.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has favorable plasticity and machinability.
The moderate hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are primarily caused by the absence of nanoscale short-range chemical order.
In high-entropy alloys, chemical ordering can increase strength by creating barriers to dislocation motion.
Ordering-induced strengthening generally increases hardness at the cost of ductility.
The absence of short-range order in CoCrFeNiTi permits relatively easy dislocation glide.
Easy dislocation glide produces the combination of moderate hardness and strength with high ductility and machinability in CoCrFeNiTi.
Aging equimolar CoCrFeNiTi at approximately 400 °C for 24 hours can induce measurable nanoscale short-range order without forming secondary phases.
Local atomic rearrangements produced by short-range ordering act as dislocation-pinning centers analogous to antiphase boundaries.
Induced short-range order will increase dislocation resistance in aged CoCrFeNiTi.
Aged CoCrFeNiTi containing short-range order will have significantly higher hardness and compressive yield strength than the as-solutionized control.
Aged CoCrFeNiTi containing short-range order will have lower compressive ductility than the as-solutionized control.
Secondary-phase precipitation could independently alter the alloy's strength and plasticity and therefore must be excluded.
The proposed comparison keeps composition, specimen geometry, and the single-phase state constant while varying the aging treatment.
The hypothesis is limited to compression of equimolar, single-phase CoCrFeNiTi at 25 °C and 600 °C.
If verified short-range order produces neither a statistically significant strength and hardness increase nor a measurable ductility decrease, the hypothesis is falsified.
